title: JavaScript Fundamentals and Advanced JavaScript
description: Master the language that powers the web — from variables and functions to closures, asynchronous code, and the modern ES6+ features used in every professional codebase.
objectives: Declare and transform data with confidence
Explain scope, closures, and the function lifecycle
Write correct asynchronous code with promises and async/await
Apply modern ES6+ syntax in real projects

modules.title: Language Fundamentals
modules.description: Values, types, variables, and control flow — the vocabulary of the language.
modules.completionCriteria: Write a small script that reads input, transforms it through conditionals and loops, and formats the output.

content.introduction: Every JavaScript program manipulates values. Knowing what type a value is — and how types convert — prevents entire categories of bugs.
content.explanation: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, and symbol, plus the object type for everything else. Variables declared with const cannot be reassigned and should be the default; let is for values that genuinely change. Avoid var entirely — it is function-scoped and hoists in surprising ways. Beware that typeof null returns "object", a quirk baked into the language, so check for null explicitly when you need to distinguish it.

examples.title: Declaring values
examples.walkthrough: TAX_RATE never changes so it is const; total is reassigned so it uses let. toFixed formats the number as a string.

content.useCase: Pricing calculations, form validation, and formatting values for display.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which declaration should be your default for a value that never changes?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: const signals intent and prevents accidental reassignment.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does typeof null return?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A historical bug in the language; use an explicit null check instead.

content.summary: Prefer const, use let when reassigning, and remember types can surprise you — especially null.

lessons.title: Operators and Type Coercion
objectives: Predict the result of mixed-type operations

content.introduction: JavaScript converts between types automatically. Understanding when — and refusing to rely on it — makes your code predictable.
content.explanation: The == operator converts operands before comparing, so "1" == 1 is true, while === compares without conversion and is almost always what you want. Addition is where coercion bites hardest: + concatenates strings, so 1 + "1" gives "11", but - * / coerce the string back to a number. Use Number(), String(), and Boolean() for explicit conversion rather than hoping the engine does what you intended. Truthiness also matters: 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN are all falsy.

examples.title: Loose vs strict equality
examples.code:
console.log("1" == 1);   // true  — converts first
console.log("1" === 1);  // false — types differ
console.log(1 + "1");    // "11"  — string concatenation
console.log("6" - 2);    // 4     — numeric subtraction
console.log(Boolean(0));  // false
examples.walkthrough: Only === and !== avoid surprise conversions. The - operator coerces to number, but + does not when either side is a string.

content.useCase: Comparing form input, URL query params, and API responses that arrive as strings.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which comparison operator avoids type coercion?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Strict equality compares both value and type.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the result of 1 + "1"?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The + operator concatenates when either operand is a string.

content.summary: Use === for comparisons and convert types explicitly instead of relying on coercion.

content.introduction: Loops decide what runs and when. Modern JavaScript gives you declarative alternatives that express intent directly.
content.explanation: for...of iterates values, for...in iterates keys, and the classic for loop remains right when you need the index or custom stepping. For arrays, prefer map to transform, filter to select, find to locate a single match, and reduce to accumulate. These methods never mutate the original array (unless you deliberately reach for forEach plus assignment), and they read as a description of the data pipeline rather than bookkeeping. Reach for a plain loop only when the logic truly needs manual control of iteration.

examples.title: A data pipeline
examples.walkthrough: filter keeps paid orders, map extracts totals, reduce sums them. The initial value 0 makes reduce safe on an empty array.

content.useCase: Summing carts, selecting matching records, and transforming API data for display.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which method transforms every element into a new array?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: map returns a new array of the same length with transformed values.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why pass 0 as the initial value to reduce?
options: It makes the reduction safe on empty arrays
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Without an initial value, reduce throws on an empty array.

content.summary: Express iteration as a pipeline: filter to select, map to transform, reduce to accumulate.

modules.title: Functions, Scope, and Closures
modules.description: How functions capture their environment — the concept behind most advanced patterns.
modules.completionCriteria: Implement a counter and a memoized function using closures, explaining what each captures.

content.introduction: Scope determines which variables a piece of code can see. In JavaScript, scope is created by functions and blocks, not by indentation.
content.explanation: A variable declared inside a function or a pair of curly braces is local to it; anything outside is global, which you should avoid. let and const are block-scoped and exist in a temporal dead zone from the block start until their declaration — reading them earlier throws. var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined, which is why older code produces surprising results. Each function call creates its own scope, so recursive calls and callbacks do not clobber each other's locals.

examples.title: Block scope vs function scope
examples.walkthrough: var ignores the block; let and const stop at the closing brace. Declaring them inside the block keeps intent local.

content.useCase: Keeping helper variables private inside a function instead of polluting global state.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which keyword is block-scoped?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: let and const are confined to the enclosing block; var is function-scoped.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the temporal dead zone?
options: The region before a let/const declaration where access throws
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The binding exists but cannot be read until execution reaches its declaration.

content.summary: Prefer let and const for block scope; avoid var and avoid globals.

content.introduction: A closure is a function together with the variables that were in scope when it was created. Those variables stay alive as long as the function does.
content.explanation: When you return an inner function, it keeps a reference to its enclosing scope's bindings even after the outer function has finished. This is not a memory leak — it is the mechanism behind private state, factories, event handlers, and hooks. Because each call to the outer function creates a fresh scope, every returned function gets its own independent copy of the captured variables, which is exactly how a counter can hold its own tally.

examples.title: A private counter
examples.walkthrough: count lives in createCounter's scope. The returned functions close over it, and each createCounter call gets its own.

content.useCase: Private counters, configuration factories, and debounced event handlers.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does a closure capture?
options: The variables in scope where the function was created
Only the arguments passed at call time
Nothing — closures do not exist in JS
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The function keeps a live reference to its lexical environment.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why do the two counters above stay independent?
options: Each createCounter call creates a new scope
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Fresh bindings are created on every invocation of the factory.

content.summary: Closures keep an enclosing scope alive — the foundation of private state and factories.

content.introduction: Arrow functions are shorter to write and differ from ordinary functions in one important way: they do not have their own `this`.
content.explanation: An arrow function inherits `this` from the surrounding scope at definition time, which eliminates the classic problem of losing context inside callbacks. That makes them ideal for handlers and array methods, and wrong for object methods that need `this` to refer to the object, or for constructors, which arrows cannot be used with. They also lack their own arguments object and cannot be used with new.

examples.title: this preserved in a callback
examples.walkthrough: The arrow keeps this bound to cart, so this.items resolves correctly inside reduce.

content.useCase: Event handlers, timers, and array pipelines where you need the outer this.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where does an arrow function get its `this`?
options: From the object it is called on
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Arrows are lexically bound; they ignore call-site this.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which use case is a poor fit for an arrow function?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Arrows have no prototype and cannot be constructed.

content.summary: Arrows inherit this lexically — perfect for callbacks, unsuitable as constructors.

modules.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
modules.description: The event loop, promises, and async/await — writing code that waits without freezing.
modules.completionCriteria: Write an async function that fetches data, handles failure, and runs independent requests in parallel.

lessons.title: The Event Loop and Callbacks
objectives: Describe the call stack and task queue

content.explanation: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack. When an operation such as a timer or network request completes, its callback is placed in a queue rather than run immediately. The event loop checks whether the stack is empty and, if so, pulls the next callback from the queue onto the stack. This is why blocking the stack with a long synchronous loop freezes the entire page — timers and clicks wait behind it. Microtasks (promise callbacks) are drained before macrotasks (timers), which is why a promise resolves before a setTimeout of 0.
content.introduction: JavaScript does one thing at a time. Asynchronous work is handled by queueing callbacks and running them when the stack is free.

examples.title: Execution order
examples.walkthrough: Synchronous logs run first. The promise microtask is drained before the timer macrotask even with a 0ms delay.

content.useCase: Reasoning about why UI updates appear out of order, and why a spinner can freeze.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens if you block the call stack with a long loop?
options: The page freezes — queued callbacks cannot run
Timers run in parallel on another thread
knowledgeCheck.explanation: There is only one thread; nothing else can run until the stack clears.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which runs first: a promise callback or setTimeout(..., 0)?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Microtasks are drained before the next macrotask.

content.summary: One thread, a queue, and an event loop that runs callbacks when the stack is empty.

content.introduction: A promise represents a value that may arrive later — and guarantees a settled outcome exactly once.
content.explanation: A promise starts pending and becomes either fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. then handles success, catch handles failure, and finally runs either way. Chaining works because then returns a new promise, letting you flatten nested operations into a linear sequence. Two rules prevent the classic bugs: always return from inside then so the value propagates, and attach a catch to every chain — an unhandled rejection fails silently in older environments. Use Promise.all to run operations in parallel and fail fast, or Promise.allSettled when you want every outcome.

examples.title: Chaining and parallel work
examples.walkthrough: The ok check converts HTTP errors into rejections. Promise.all starts both requests together and rejects if either fails.

content.useCase: Fetching several resources at once and showing a single error state on failure.

knowledgeCheck.question: How many times can a promise settle?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Later attempts to resolve or reject are ignored.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does Promise.all do when one input rejects?
options: It waits for all to finish
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Use Promise.allSettled if you need every result regardless of failure.

content.summary: Promises settle once, chain linearly, and support parallel execution with Promise.all.

lessons.title: async/await
objectives: Write sequential and parallel async code

content.introduction: async/await is syntax over promises that lets asynchronous code read like ordinary synchronous code.
content.explanation: An async function always returns a promise, and await pauses that function — not the whole thread — until the awaited promise settles. Sequential awaits express order clearly, but they are slow when operations are independent: awaiting them one by one runs them serially. For independent work, start them all first and await the combined promise. Errors surface as thrown exceptions, so wrap the flow in try/catch; note that a try/catch does not catch errors from a floating promise you never awaited.

examples.title: Sequential vs parallel
examples.walkthrough: Destructuring the Promise.all result keeps both values. try/catch handles any rejection from either request.

content.useCase: Any page that needs several independent API calls before rendering.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does await actually pause?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Other code, including timers, keeps running normally.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why run independent requests with Promise.all?
options: They execute concurrently instead of serially
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Awaiting them one after another adds each duration together.

content.summary: await pauses one function; start independent work together and catch errors with try/catch.

modules.title: Advanced JavaScript Patterns
modules.description: Objects, prototypes, modules, and the tools that keep large codebases maintainable.
modules.completionCriteria: Explain prototypal inheritance and organize a script into explicit module exports.

lessons.title: Objects and Prototypes
objectives: Trace property lookup along the prototype chain

content.introduction: JavaScript objects inherit from other objects. Property lookup walks that chain until it finds a match or reaches the end.
content.explanation: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link. When a property is missing on the object itself, JavaScript checks its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, and so on — the prototype chain. Methods like toString are found this way on Object.prototype. The class syntax is syntactic sugar over this mechanism: methods defined in a class body live on the prototype and are shared by every instance, while fields assigned in the constructor are per-instance. Understanding this explains why methods are not duplicated in memory and why instanceof works.

examples.title: Prototype lookup
examples.walkthrough: speak is found on Dog. The instance still links to Animal through the chain, so instanceof holds for both.

content.useCase: Sharing behavior across many instances without duplicating methods.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where are class methods stored?
options: On the prototype, shared by all instances
knowledgeCheck.explanation: This is why methods are not re-created for every object.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does d instanceof Animal check?
options: Whether Animal.prototype appears in the chain
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It walks the prototype chain looking for Animal.prototype.

content.summary: Property lookup walks the prototype chain; classes are sugar over prototypal inheritance.

content.introduction: Modules let you split a program into files with explicit imports and exports, instead of relying on global scripts.
content.explanation: ES modules use export to expose values and import to consume them. Named exports suit several values from one file and make refactoring safer because the binding name matters; a default export suits a file whose primary purpose is one component or function. Imports are live bindings — if the exporting module changes the value, importers see it — and they are also hoisted, so a module's dependencies load before its own code runs. Modules execute once regardless of how many files import them, which makes them a natural place for shared singletons.

examples.title: Named and default exports
examples.walkthrough: Named exports are imported by exact name; the default export can be given any local name.

content.useCase: Sharing utilities, API clients, and constants across files without globals.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a benefit of named exports over a single global script?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: You can see exactly what each file depends on by reading its imports.

knowledgeCheck.question: How many default exports may one module have?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Use named exports when you need to expose several values.

content.summary: Modules make dependencies explicit. Prefer named exports for shared utilities.

content.introduction: Anything that works with for...of follows a small protocol. Generators are the easiest way to implement it.
content.explanation: An iterable exposes a method returning an iterator with next(), which yields { value, done }. Arrays, strings, and Maps are all iterables. A generator function marked with * and containing yield produces an iterator automatically, computing values lazily — only when asked. That makes generators ideal for infinite or very large sequences, pausing expensive work, and implementing custom iteration without hand-writing the protocol. Because state is preserved between yields, a generator can also model resumable workflows.

examples.title: A lazy range generator
examples.walkthrough: Values are produced on demand; break stops work immediately instead of building a million-element array.

content.useCase: Paginating large datasets, reading streams, and representing game or workflow states.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes a value iterable?
options: It implements a method returning an iterator
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Symbol.iterator method is the actual requirement.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main benefit of generators?
options: Lazy evaluation — values are computed on demand
knowledgeCheck.explanation: They pause at each yield, so nothing is computed until requested.

content.summary: Generators implement the iterator protocol with lazy, resumable production of values.
